answer_text:
# How to Read Pregnancy Test Results

Here is a comprehensive guide to understanding your pregnancy test results:

---

## 🔬 How the Test Works

Home pregnancy tests are designed to identify the presence of a specific hormone in your urine: human chorionic gonadotropin, commonly known as hCG. hCG levels are initially very low but double approximately every 48 to 72 hours in early pregnancy.

---

## ✅ Positive Result (PREGNANT)

A pregnancy test is positive when two lines appear – one in the Control (C) region and one in the Test (T) region. Even if the second line is faint, it still indicates the presence of hCG hormone, confirming pregnancy.

- Digital pregnancy tests are the easiest to read — the result window will clearly say **"Pregnant"** or **"Yes"** if you're pregnant.
- Single test windows will show **two lines side-by-side** if your test is positive. One line is the control line, and the second line is the result line. Two-window tests will show a line in the smaller control window and a **plus "+" sign** in the larger, second window.

---

## ❌ Negative Result (NOT PREGNANT)

A **negative result** means only one color band appears on the top Control (C) region, with no apparent band on the Test (T) region.

- A digital test will say **"Not Pregnant"** or **"No"** if you're not pregnant.

---

## ⚠️ Invalid Result

If no line appears, or there's only one line in the (T) and not in the (C), the test is **invalid**. A blurry or unreadable test window also indicates invalid results. If there is no visible control line, discard the test and repeat with a new device.

---

## 🔍 What About a Faint Line?

In the vast majority of cases, **a faint line is a positive line**. It indicates that hCG is present, but the concentration in your urine may still be relatively low — this is typical in very early pregnancy.

If you see a faint line, you should consider yourself pregnant and confirm with another test in a few days, when the line will likely be darker.

---

## 🕐 Evaporation Lines (False Positive Look-alike)

An evaporation line (or "evap line") is a faint, colorless streak that can appear in the test window **after** the urine has dried and the designated reading time has passed. It is **not** a positive result — it is a residue left by the evaporated urine.

Distinguishing faint lines from evaporation lines comes down to **timing and color**. A faint positive line will appear within the recommended window of time (usually within three to five minutes) and will activate the dye in the pregnancy test, so it can appear blue or light pink in color.

---

## ⏰ When & How to Take the Test for Best Accuracy

| Tip | Details |
|-----|---------|
| **Best time to test** | For the most reliable result, test on the day of your missed period or later. |
| **Best time of day** | For the most accurate result, use your **first-morning urine**, which is typically more concentrated and contains the highest level of hCG. |
| **Reading time** | Read your test between **5 and 10 minutes** after taking it. Beyond that window, you may see an evaporation line which isn't the same as a positive. |

---

## ❗ False Results

- **False Negative:** This is when the test reads negative, but you are actually pregnant. Common causes include testing too early, diluted urine, not following instructions correctly, reading the test too soon or too late, or an expired test.

- **False Positive:** This is a much rarer occurrence — when the test reads positive, but you are not pregnant. Common causes include certain medications containing hCG (used in fertility treatments), recent miscarriage or abortion, rare medical conditions like ovarian cysts or certain cancers, an evaporation line mistakenly interpreted as positive, or a faulty test.

---

## 🩺 Next Steps

- All results should be **confirmed by a doctor**, especially when making decisions about future medical care.
- If your pregnancy test is negative, but you still don't get your period in two days, **take another test**.
- A home pregnancy test is a **screening tool** and should not be used as the only basis for diagnosis. Your healthcare provider should confirm pregnancy based on a full clinical evaluation.
